stops.title: Pick a lane while nobody is pushing you
stops.silver: Without the rules you cannot look ahead from a spot to see where each key takes you. So you keep a score on every move from every spot, and getting better just means pressing whichever move scores highest.
stops.do: The game asks which lane pays more when nothing pushes you: LEFT CLICK for EDGE, RIGHT CLICK for INLAND, MELEE for THE SAME. Then LEFT CLICK or RIGHT CLICK picks your lane, and you walk it with WASD from the white ring to the green ring.
stops.predict: Commit to which lane earns more when every step goes where you aim it.
stops.saw: Edge 39, inland 37. Each pad costs 1, the goal pays 50, and the edge is two pads shorter. With nothing pushing you, reading off the higher score picks the short way, and the short way is right. Silver builds his whole loop on this one step: greedy improvement on action values.
stops.agent: Score a plan as if every tool call does exactly what you meant, and the one with the fewest steps always looks best. Hold that thought until Lucio shows up.

stops.title: Lucio arrives: one step in ten
stops.silver: To stop a learner locking onto its first good guess, Silver makes one move in ten a random one. He calls it epsilon-greedy. It is the cheap cure for the teammate who only ever takes one flank.
stops.do: Lucio now stands inland. The game asks the chance that one step off an edge pad ends over the drop: LEFT CLICK, RIGHT CLICK or MELEE for the three answers. Then pick a lane and walk it.
stops.predict: Commit to how likely a single edge step is to send you over, before you take one.
stops.saw: One step in ten is swapped for a random one of four moves, and one of those four points at the drop. So each edge step goes over 1 time in 40. Lucio is the lecture's random move, made for you. Check the right side: how many boops you took, and where they sent you.
stops.agent: Sampling with some randomness makes a model try other actions now and then, and other actions include the ones that cannot be undone.

stops.title: Count the falls along the edge
stops.silver: Silver wants exploring that never stops but fades: every move keeps getting tried, and the learner still locks in on the best one in the end.
stops.do: The game asks how often the whole edge lane ends in a fall with boops on: LEFT CLICK, RIGHT CLICK or MELEE. Then pick a lane and walk it again.
stops.predict: Commit to roughly how many crossings in 100 end over the drop if you always take the edge.
stops.saw: Eleven edge steps at 1 in 40 each comes to about 24 falls in 100. Count the walks back after other boops and the game's own arithmetic says about 26. Here the boops never fade, so that tax never shrinks. A schedule that lowers the random share over time, which Silver calls GLIE, is what would let it fall toward zero.
stops.agent: An agent with a fixed amount of randomness pays the same tax for it on every run, however much it has learned.

stops.title: Which lane wins in the long run
stops.silver: SARSA nudges the score of what you just did toward the reward plus the score of the move you will really make next, random moves included. It is honest about how you actually play.
stops.do: The game asks which lane earns more on average with boops on: LEFT CLICK for EDGE, RIGHT CLICK for INLAND. The answer and both averages appear, and then you pick a lane for the last crossing and walk it.
stops.predict: Commit to the lane that earns more over many crossings when Lucio is around.
stops.saw: Edge 0.41, inland 30.31. A 26 in 100 chance of losing 100 costs far more than two extra pads. These are the scores of the walker who really gets booped, which is what SARSA learns, so SARSA walks inland. Hold your own four returns on the right up against those averages.
stops.agent: Score a strategy by the runs the agent actually produces, slips and all, and the cautious route often wins.

stops.title: Name the learner that hugs the edge
stops.silver: Q-learning nudges the score of what you did toward the reward plus the best score available where you landed, whatever you actually do next. It rates every spot as if your next move will be perfect.
stops.do: The game asks which learner ends up preferring the edge: LEFT CLICK for Q-LEARNING, RIGHT CLICK for SARSA. A short reveal follows on the coach line.
stops.predict: Using lecture 4's rule (move a guess toward the reward plus the next guess), commit to which next guess makes the edge look best.
stops.saw: The best next move is never a boop, so Q-learning scores the edge at 39 and keeps walking it. SARSA counts the boops and scores it 0.41. Q-learning learns about the player you could be while playing as the one you are: off-policy. SARSA learns about the one you are: on-policy.
stops.agent: Training on what a flawless version would do, while the real agent still slips, is the Q-learning choice. A good map, carried by a walker who trips.

stops.title: Read the debrief
stops.silver: Silver goes straight past the cliff-walk slide without a word. Its plot says it for him: the careful learner earns more while it learns, and the edge-hugging learner falls more.
stops.do: Nothing to press. Read the three debrief lines and your prediction score in the left block; the right block keeps your four crossings and the long-run averages.
stops.predict: Before reading, say to yourself which of your four crossings you would repeat.
stops.saw: You crossed beside a drop while getting booped, and the arithmetic showed the short lane losing once the boops were counted. One honest limit: here the boop stands in for your own random move. If the boops belonged to the world itself, Q-learning would learn them too and would also move inland.
stops.agent: Judge a plan by what your agent will really do, mistakes included, not by what a perfect run would score.
